Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN)  -- Coalition forces found 26 bodies buried in mass graves and a bloodstained "torture complex," with chains hanging from walls and ceilings and a bed connected to an electrical system, the military said Wednesday. Twenty-six bodies were found in mass graves near a "torture complex" discovered by coalition forces. The troops made the discovery while conducting an operation north of Muqdadiya, Iraq. From December 8 to 11, the troops who found the complex also killed 24 people they said were terrorists and detained 37 suspects, according to a statement issued by Multinational Division North at Camp Speicher in Tikrit. The moves were part of an operation called Iron Reaper that has been in progress across northern Iraq for the past few weeks. The complex was in an area thought to be an al Qaeda in Iraq haven and operating base, the military said. Iraqis had told the military about the site during an earlier operation. "Evidence of murder, torture and intimidation against local villagers was found throughout the area," the military statement said. Ground forces first found what appeared to be a detention facility, which was one of three connected to the torture complex, Multinational Division North said. One of the facilities appeared to have been a headquarters building and a torture facility, it added. As the area was cleared, the bodies were found. Eventually, 26 bodies were uncovered in mass graves next to what were thought to be execution sites, the military said. The bodies are believed to have been dead between six and eight months, according to a gruesome military video shot at the scene. Some had their hands tied behind their backs. Identification is proving to be a challenge because of advanced decomposition. Photos given to the news media show a filthy bed wired to an electrical system, with an outlet hanging from wires on the wall. In the video, troops point out rubber hoses and boxing gloves, a ski mask and a blood-covered sword and knives. Other still photos show an entrance to the underground bunker and barbed wire stretched outside it. A short distance away from the complex, troops found a bullet-riddled Iraqi police vehicle. Some of the bodies may belong to Iraqi police, according to the military video. The operation netted nine weapons caches, which have been destroyed, the military said. They included anti-aircraft weapons, sniper rifles, more than 65 machine guns and pistols, 50 grenades and a surface-to-air missile launcher and platform, the statement said. Also found were mines, pipe bombs, rocket-propelled grenades, mortar tubes and rounds and 130 pounds of homemade explosives. E-mail to a friend .

The discovery was made during an operation conducted north of Muqdadiya, Iraq. Between December 8 and 11, the troops responsible for finding the complex also killed 24 individuals identified as terrorists and detained 37 suspects, according to a statement from Multinational Division North at Camp Speicher in Tikrit.

These actions formed part of Operation Iron Reaper, which has been underway across northern Iraq for several weeks. The military identified the area as a suspected haven and operating base for al Qaeda in Iraq, noting that local Iraqis had provided information about the site during a previous operation.

"Evidence of murder, torture and intimidation against local villagers was found throughout the area," the military statement said.

Ground forces initially discovered what appeared to be a detention facility—one of three structures connected to the torture complex, according to Multinational Division North. One of these facilities is believed to have served as both a headquarters and a torture site. As troops cleared the area, they uncovered 26 bodies in mass graves situated near suspected execution sites.

Military video footage taken at the scene suggests the bodies had been buried for six to eight months, with some victims' hands bound behind their backs. Advanced decomposition has complicated identification efforts.

Photographs released to the media depict a soiled bed connected to electrical wiring, with an exposed outlet dangling from the wall. Video footage further reveals rubber hoses, boxing gloves, a ski mask, and a blood-stained sword and knives. Additional photos show the entrance to an underground bunker encircled by barbed wire.

Not far from the complex, troops discovered a bullet-riddled Iraqi police vehicle, and military footage suggests some of the recovered bodies may belong to Iraqi police officers.

The broader operation resulted in the discovery and destruction of nine weapons caches. These included anti-aircraft weapons, sniper rifles, more than 65 machine guns and pistols, 50 grenades, and a surface-to-air missile launcher with its platform, according to the statement. Additional items recovered included mines, pipe bombs, rocket-propelled grenades, mortar tubes and rounds, and 130 pounds of homemade explosives.

# Coalition Forces Uncover Suspected al Qaeda Torture Complex North of Muqdadiya

Coalition forces conducting Operation Iron Reaper in the volatile region north of Muqdadiya, Iraq, have uncovered what military officials are calling a suspected al Qaeda "torture complex," revealing disturbing evidence of a systematic campaign of murder, intimidation, and abuse against local villagers.

The grim discovery came after local residents, apparently emboldened to come forward, tipped off coalition troops operating in the area about the existence of the facility. Acting on this intelligence, soldiers moved into the site and found a complex that appeared to have been purpose-built for detaining and interrogating captives. Investigators discovered chains used to restrain victims, as well as what has been described as an electrified bed—apparently employed as a device for inflicting pain during interrogations. Numerous weapons recovered from the site bore visible bloodstains, further reinforcing suspicions that the location had been used for brutal and prolonged abuse of detainees.

Perhaps most disturbing was the discovery of mass graves in the vicinity of the complex. Search teams uncovered the remains of 26 individuals buried near what are believed to be former execution sites associated with the facility. Military officials noted that identifying the victims has proven extremely difficult, as many of the remains have significantly decomposed, complicating efforts to determine who they were, when they died, or how long the site had been in operation.

The uncovering of the torture complex coincided with broader combat operations in the area as part of Iron Reaper. During the course of the operation, coalition and Iraqi forces reported killing 24 individuals identified as alleged terrorists, while detaining an additional 37 suspects believed to be linked to insurgent or al Qaeda activity in the region.

Military officials characterized the find as powerful, if grim, evidence of the tactics allegedly employed by al Qaeda in Iraq to control local populations through fear. The presence of detention cells, interrogation equipment, and nearby burial sites suggests a deliberate and sustained effort to terrorize villagers in the surrounding area, using torture and extrajudicial killing as tools of intimidation against anyone suspected of cooperating with coalition or Iraqi government forces.

While the operation has yielded significant intelligence and dealt a blow to insurgent operations in the region, the discovery of the torture complex underscores the human cost of the ongoing conflict. Efforts to identify the victims found in the mass graves are expected to continue, though officials caution that the state of decomposition may make definitive identification impossible in many cases. Coalition forces indicated that the site would be further examined for any additional evidence that could aid in identifying both the victims and those responsible for the atrocities committed there.

Forensic and human rights teams, including representatives from international organizations, are expected to begin a more thorough excavation of the burial sites in coming days. Officials cautioned that establishing an accurate count of victims could take weeks or months, given the condition of the remains and the scope of the site.

This discovery adds to a growing number of similar sites uncovered across Iraq since the fall of the former government, as investigators work to document abuses committed over the preceding decades. *Baghdad* — U.S. and coalition forces investigating a suspected detention and interrogation site near Tikrit have uncovered what military officials describe as evidence of systematic executions and torture, according to a statement released by Coalition officials Thursday.

Troops conducting a raid on a compound roughly 15 miles outside the city discovered a mass grave containing the remains of an estimated 20 to 30 individuals, many showing signs of gunshot wounds to the back of the head consistent with summary execution. Forensic teams have been dispatched to the site to begin exhumation and identification procedures, a process officials cautioned could take weeks given the condition of the remains.

Inside an adjacent building, soldiers reported finding what appeared to be an improvised interrogation chamber. Items recovered from the scene included metal restraints bolted to concrete walls, car batteries wired with clamps, lengths of rubber hose, and blindfolds. Blood stains were visible on the floor and walls of several rooms, according to a military spokesperson who briefed reporters on condition of anonymity pending a fuller forensic assessment.

"What we're seeing here fits a pattern we've encountered elsewhere in the region," the spokesperson said. "Rooms set up specifically for the purpose of extracting information or confessions through pain, followed in some cases by killing."

Coalition forces detained six individuals present at or near the compound at the time of the raid, including a man identified by local residents as a former mid-level security official under the previous government. Military officials said the detainees are being held for questioning and that charges have not yet been filed pending further investigation.

Local residents interviewed near the site said the compound had been used for "unofficial" detentions for years, though few were willing to speak in detail, citing fear of reprisal even after the change in government. One elderly man, who declined to give his name, said a relative had disappeared after being taken to a facility in the area in the 1990s and was never seen again.

Coalition officials said the findings would be turned over to Iraqi judicial authorities as part of a broader effort to document abuses for potential future prosecutions. Similar mass graves and detention sites have been discovered in other parts of the country since the fall of the previous government, though officials noted that each new site requires independent verification before conclusions can be drawn about the scale or timing of the killings.

Human rights investigators are expected to arrive at the Tikrit site in the coming days to assist with documentation and to interview witnesses. No official death toll has been confirmed, and officials stressed that the investigation remains in its early stages.
